articles.title: Week of Oct. 19 Evening News Ratings: All Broadcasts Grow
articles.fullContent:
By Mark Mwachiro The three evening newscasts all recorded week-to-week growth in total viewers and the Adults 25-54 demo. ABC World News Tonight with David Muir maintained its status as the most-watched news broadcast in both measures. For the week of October 19, WNT delivered its largest total viewer performance since the week of March 2, 2026.

Meanwhile, CBS Evening News with Tony Dokoupil also had a strong week, posting double-digit growth in total viewers. It was the only telecast to see its weekly viewership grow by double figures.

Note: The weekly averages of ABC News, NBC News, and CBS News are based on different periods: NBC News’ average is based on three days (Monday – Wednesday), while ABC News’ and CBS News’ averages are based on four days (Monday – Thursday). Tuesday’s (10/20/26) NBC News broadcast was retitled to NBC Nitely News. Friday’s (10/23/26) ABC News and CBS News’ broadcasts were retitled to WNT and CBS Evening Nws, respectively. These broadcasts were excluded from the weekly and season averages.

According to Nielsen national live+same-day big data and program ratings, ABC World News Tonight averaged 8.837 million total viewers and 1.198 million Adults 25-54 demo viewers for the week of Oct. 19. The evening newscast was up +6% in total viewers and +6% in the A25-54 demo compared to the previous week . During the same week in 2025 ( the week beginning Oct. 20 ), WNT was up +12% in total viewers and +30% in the demo.

As for NBC Nightly News, it was in second place in total viewers and the demo, averaging 6.72 million and 1.107 million viewers, respectively. Compared to the previous week, Nightly News grew by +1% in total viewers and +9% in the demo. When comparing its performance to the same week a year ago, Nightly News was up by +15% in total viewers and +38% in the demo.

Finally, CBS Evening News finished the week of Oct. 19 with 4.626 million total viewers and 688,000 demo viewers. CBS News’ newscast was up +10% in total viewers and +5% compared to the previous week. Its year-ago week numbers showed CBS Evening News up +13% in total viewers and +51% in the demo.

articles.title: Social media in education: 10 tips and benefits for 2026
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. Social media in education can boost student engagement, connect learners with global resources, and strengthen institutional branding when it’s used strategically.
  2. Risks like cyberbullying, privacy violations, and mental health impacts mean schools need clear policies alongside any social media use, plus compliance with FERPA, COPPA, and CIPA.
  3. Educators can use social media in the classroom for active learning, digital literacy development, networking skills, and community building.
  4. Tracking education-specific benchmarks helps institutions set realistic goals and show what social media is actually delivering.

What is social media in education?

Social media in education is the use of platforms like YouTube, Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn, Facebook, and X for teaching, learning, and institutional communication. It generally covers two distinct things, and it helps to keep them separate.

The first is social media as a classroom tool: assignments, discussion prompts, livestreamed lectures, digital literacy lessons, and collaboration between students. The second is social media as an institutional channel: recruitment campaigns, campus alerts, alumni relations, and brand building.

Both matter because students are already there. Nine-in-ten U.S. teens say they use YouTube, with majorities also on TikTok and Instagram. Meeting students on the platforms they use daily is usually easier than pulling them somewhere else.

What are the benefits of social media in education?

Used well, social media can make classrooms more engaged and institutions more connected. The main benefits:

  • Student engagement: Reaching learners on platforms they already use
  • Global access: Connecting students with experts and perspectives beyond campus
  • Collaboration: Easier communication between students, and between students and teachers
  • Professional development: Peer learning communities for educators

How does social media increase student engagement?

Social media increases student engagement by meeting learners on platforms they already use. Normally, when we discuss “engagement,” we’re referring to likes, comments, and shares on a social media post. However, “engagement” can have a double meaning when using social media in education.

Student engagement is key to a successful classroom. When students are engaged, curious, and social in class, it shows that you are succeeding as an educator.

Social media resources can help facilitate and encourage engagement with your students. When teens are spending 1 hour and 18 minutes per day on TikTok alone, bringing those platforms into the classroom helps you meet them where they already are rather than competing for their attention.

How does social media provide access to global resources and expert perspectives?

Social media lets students connect with anyone around the world. One of the best things to come out of social media is this ability, and it has a benefit in the classroom, too, especially for higher education programs.

You can connect students with global resources and experts to help broaden their perspectives. Host an Instagram Live with an expert or have students connect with professionals on LinkedIn to enhance their learning experience.

How does social media improve communication and collaboration?

Social media improves communication because most students are already comfortable using it. It only makes sense to bring that communication method into the classroom.

Social media can be a great way to facilitate conversations around lessons or collaborations for group projects. Think private Facebook Groups or Slack channels. Students can also build their collaborative skills with document-sharing tools like Google Docs. Groups of students can share notes and collaborate during lessons in real time.

It’s not just great for students, either. Social media can help build relationships between teachers and students, making it easier to communicate with students about classroom updates or other discussions.

How does social media support professional development for educators?

Social media supports professional development by giving educators a low-cost way to learn from peers. Inviting, rather than resisting, social media into your classroom can have huge benefits. Use it to promote collaboration, share resources and ideas, and provide real-time feedback.

Teacher communities on LinkedIn, Facebook, and Reddit regularly share lesson plans, classroom management tactics, and engagement methods. It’s a way to learn from peers in other districts and institutions without waiting for a conference.

What are the risks and challenges of social media in education?

Social media brings real risks into school environments, and most of them are manageable with the right policies. The ones educators and administrators should plan for:

  • Cyberbullying: Harassment that follows students home and is harder for staff to see
  • Privacy violations: Sharing student names, images, or records without consent can breach federal law
  • Misinformation: Students encounter unverified claims faster than they can evaluate them
  • Distraction: Phones and feeds compete directly with instruction time,...

articles.title: Your Marketing Playbook Expired Last Week ft. Erin Oles of Salesforce
articles.fullContent:
By Jenny Rooney If you’re wondering why your good ol’ marketing playbook no longer works, the answer probably lies in the funnel you’re targeting.

Recorded live at Advertising Week New York, this episode of Marketing Vanguard features Jenny Rooney in conversation with Salesforce CMO Erin Oles to unpack what happens when customer behavior moves faster than the funnel marketers built around it.

Erin gets into why traditional attribution assumptions are starting to crack and what it takes to map tomorrow’s customer journey.

She also addresses why marketers need to understand how their brand appears inside LLMs and why AI should be given real problems instead of vague “use cases.”

Why Erin thinks the idea of a fixed marketing “playbook” is becoming an oxymoron

Why buyer behavior is making the traditional nurture funnel feel increasingly artificial

Why yesterday’s attribution models may not explain tomorrow’s customer journey

Why AEO is not simply SEO with a new acronym

How owned content can quietly work against your brand inside LLM results

Why AI works best when you start with a problem instead of a tool

Why context becomes more valuable as access to intelligence becomes more universal

How AI-driven discovery could push marketers beyond the traditional boundaries of marketing

Erin Oles is CMO at Salesforce. Her path into marketing began in sales, an experience she credits with teaching her how quickly you can tell whether a message actually resonates with a real person.

Today, her approach to AI is similarly practical. Rather than treating new technology as something marketers need to master in theory, Erin argues for learning by doing, staying anchored to customer problems and handing repetitive work to AI when human judgment can be better spent elsewhere.

At Salesforce, that means rethinking everything from AI search visibility and customer discovery to conversational agents and real-time campaign optimization.

[02:40] Your Marketing Playbook Has a One-Week Shelf Life — Erin jokes that calling something a “marketing playbook” is almost an oxymoron now. Her point is that customer behavior is shifting too quickly for marketers to assume the same funnel mechanics will keep working. Instead of obsessing over getting buyers onto owned properties and into nurture, marketers have to become useful and credible wherever discovery actually happens.

[05:38] Your Own Website Might Be Working Against You — Erin shares a brutal finding from an event with 30 CMOs: every participant, including her, had owned properties actively working against them in LLM results. She further points to a wider gap between CMOs who say AI visibility matters and those actually using what they learn to change their marketing. The lesson is uncomfortable: your AI-search problem may be coming from content you already own.

[11:04] Give AI a Problem, Not a Use Case — Erin’s clearest AI rule is refreshingly practical: start with the problem. Salesforce created an SEO agent that found 10,000 broken links and pages across owned web properties, work Erin estimates would have taken roughly 5,000 human hours. AI handled it within hours. The win was not “using AI.” The win was giving people thousands of hours back for work that actually needs human judgment.

[13:47] Stop Forcing Buyers Through a Funnel They Never Asked For — The old funnel assumes marketers can get buyers to identify themselves, arrive on an owned property and move neatly through nurture. Erin argues that behavior increasingly does not look like that. Buyers are researching through LLMs, talking to peers and moving between sources before a brand ever sees them. Her answer is “surround marketing”: build enough relevance and credibility around the customer that you matter wherever they choose to look.

Jenny Rooney is Chief Brand and Community Officer, leading strategy for the overall ADWEEK brand as well as the ways in which we serve and support our audiences with high-value content, products, partnerships and experiences, notably through our community programs such as Marketing Vanguard.

articles.title: Avoiding The Ick Factor: Anthony Po and Lauren Probyn Aouad on Getting Authenticity Right
articles.fullContent:
By Adweek Staff What makes a brand stand out in a crowded digital landscape, capture attention, and create campaigns that genuinely resonate? It starts with understanding culture, not chasing virality.

In this episode of Adspeak by ADWEEK, host Lauren Probyn Aouad, VP of entertainment & culture marketing at UTA, sits down with Anthony Po, creator, performance artist, and co-founder of Pufferfish.

Recorded live at Brandweek 2026 , the conversation explores how creators are redefining brand marketing, why authenticity matters more than strategy alone, and what it takes to turn cultural moments into meaningful audience connections.

The discussion examines why copying viral campaigns rarely works, how brands can recognize the “ick factor” that makes audiences disengage, and why marketers must earn attention before delivering their message.

Anthony also shares insights on the growing business opportunities for creators, the importance of involving culturally immersed talent, and how testing content with engaged communities can help refine campaigns before launch.

For marketers looking to connect with digital-native audiences, the conversation offers a valuable reminder: genuine cultural understanding and creativity can accomplish far more than simply chasing the next viral moment.

Why copying a viral campaign’s format (not its feeling) guarantees audience rejection and algorithmic punishment

How to identify the “ick factor” that signals to digitally native audiences you’re exploiting culture rather than participating in it

The “earn the view first” principle with creating genuine attention

Why hiring people who are actually immersed in culture is non-negotiable for authentic digital content

How to decide whether a campaign should optimize for direct conversion versus long-term brand equity

The value of pre-launching content to small, engaged fan communities for real-time feedback before a public release

Anthony Po is the co-founder of Pufferfish, a media company specializing in creator-led brand activations and cultural storytelling. With a decade-long background as a content creator across Instagram, YouTube, and TikTok, including a tenure leading short-form creative at MrBeast, Anthony  has mastered the art of building authentic connections with digitally native audiences through innovative, culture-first campaigns.

[05:20] Recreate the Feeling, Not the Viral Stunt — Viral campaigns succeed because they capture a feeling audiences connect with, not simply because of their format. Anthony explains why brands attempting to replicate stunts like the Timothée Chalamet lookalike contest often miss the point. By understanding what made the original moment resonate and creating something fresh around that emotion, marketers can participate in culture without appearing opportunistic. The goal is genuine audience connection, not imitation.

[06:37] Hire People Who Actually Live and Breathe Culture — Authentic digital marketing requires people who understand internet culture from experience, not just research. Anthony and Lauren discuss how even small details, such as font choices, can reveal whether a brand truly understands its audience. Anthony points to brands like Duolingo and Wendy’s, whose social presence reflects genuine digital fluency. For marketers, the lesson is to bring culturally immersed talent into campaign development rather than expecting disconnected teams to manufacture authenticity.

[16:01] Earn the View Before Introducing Your Brand — Content must capture attention before brand guidelines and messaging become relevant. Anthony explains how his team prioritizes entertainment, education, or practical value before worrying about custom fonts and other brand elements. This approach challenges marketers to rethink content that leads with corporate messaging and gets ignored. By earning the audience’s attention first, brands can make their presence feel natural and relevant rather than intrusive.

[17:03] Are You Driving Sales or Building Brand Equity? — Campaigns designed for immediate conversions require a different approach from those intended to build long-term brand equity. Anthony highlights why expecting one creative asset to deliver both direct sales and cultural buzz can lead to disappointing results. He recommends defining the objective before choosing the format and measurement framework. Straightforward ads may work best for conversions, while culturally resonant campaigns can build positive associations that strengthen the brand value over time.

[19:21] Test Your Content With Fans Before Going Public — Testing content with engaged communities can reveal weaknesses before a campaign reaches a wider audience. Anthony and Lauren discuss how creators use platforms like Patreon and YouTube memberships to gather feedback on early cuts and refine their work. Even when the feedback challenges his own instincts, he finds that outside perspectives improve the final product. For marketers, this offers a practical alternative to traditional focus groups and helps reduce the risk of public missteps.

articles.title: Google Recommends Using Custom 404 Error Pages via @sejournal, @martinibuster
articles.fullContent:
Googlers Gary Illyes and Cherry Sireetorn Prommawin recently explained that 404 errors aren’t an SEO problem to worry about. They recommended approaching 404s like a business problem instead, suggesting that a custom 404 error page is an ideal way to handle missing pages.

The most interesting part of the podcast is how they contextualized 404 errors as a business and user experience issue rather than a strictly technical SEO problem that needs solving. They explained that a missing web page is not in itself a search problem. They also explained that whether a site owner needs to take action depends on the value that missing page does or does not provide to website visitors.

The podcast provided four takeaways about 404 errors:

Managing missing pages is a business and user experience decision.

The appropriate response depends on whether a replacement exists.

404 errors do not consume crawl budget in the way server errors do.

Google Says 404 Errors Are Normal And Don’t Affect Rankings

Many people see 404 error reports in Google Search Console and the way it’s set up gives the impression that it’s an issue that needs taking care of. Naturally, if Google shows you something is in error the natural response is to fix it. But that’s actually not the right approach to this kind of error.

The first point they explained is that 404 errors are a natural part of the web. Pages disappear, events come and go, products are discontinued, topics become outdated and eventually URLs are deleted, usually for a good reason. Google’s Gary Illyes explained that 404 errors are generally not a problem.

“You open Search Console, see a list of 404 errors, and boom, instant panic. People think the domain will get a manual action or it will be cursed and never rank again.

Illyes answered that Google does not care if a URL is gone and is now showing a 404 error response code.

An HTTP 404 status code literally just means not found. It is a perfectly natural, healthy part of the web. Pages die, products sell out, old URLs get deleted.

Googlebot encounters a 404, realizes the page is gone, and eventually we drop it from the index. There is no penalty, no secret Google jail, and no negative impact on your other healthy pages.

From our perspective, it’s completely fine to just leave them be.”

Fixing 404 Errors Is A Business Decision, Not An SEO Requirement

What may be surprising to some SEOs is the idea that 404 errors are a business decision and not something that requires fixing for SEO purposes. What they did was remove 404 errors out of the context of SEO and recontextualized it as a business decision along the lines of whether removing a page makes sense for the website and business goals.

So rather than think of 404 errors as an SEO problem it’s actually more appropriate to think of them on the business level as in whether redirecting a URL or leaving it permanently gone makes sense for site visitors or whatever it is the website is trying to accomplish.

“Fixing a 404 is entirely optional, but it can be a smart business move, depending on your site. For example, if you run an e-commerce store and you delete a popular product page like ultimate deluxe chicken feed, leaving a blank error page means you might be dropping potential sales.”

Prommawin agreed, commenting that this is really about the user experience and less about Google Search.

“If the dead URL still gets traffic from all links or social media, you might choose to guide those users to a newer product model using a redirect.”

She next added that if there’s no replacement then the proper response is to just let the server provide a 404 error response.

Prommawin offered this additional guidance:

“Also, don’t take the lazy shortcut if you’re thinking, let’s redirect all your dead pages to the home page. That just confuses humans and make your data very confusing.”

Google’s Three-Step Approach For Managing 404 Errors

Prommawin and Illyes provided a practical decision-making approach for dealing with content and URLs that have been removed.

Step 1: Redirect Only When A Relevant Replacement Exists

They recommended using one-to-one redirects for pages that have genuinely been replaced with another page. An updated article or newer model of the same product qualifies as a relevant replacement page. They both emphasized matching the original page with a specific replacement that makes sense.

“First, one-to-one relevant directs, but only if a true replacement exists. If that page has a direct natural replacement, like an updated version of the same article or a newer model of the exact same product, you set up a redirect only to that specific, highly relevant destination.”

Step 2: Return A 404 Or 410 When No Replacement Exists

They explained that permanently deleting pages because there is no natural replacement is fine and those should return a 404 or 410 status code. Allowing Google to remove these URLs from its index is normal and has zero effect on a website’s SEO status.

articles.title: Google Says Lower AI Mode Monetization Weighed On Search Growth via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern
articles.fullContent:
Alphabet’s (GOOGL) Google Search & Other line had a 12% increase in year-over-year revenue in Q3 2026 to $63.35 billion. Search revenue growth has been slowing down for two quarters now, after being at 19% in Q1 and 17% in Q2; and Search revenue was essentially flat compared to last quarter’s $63.27 billion.

On Alphabet’s earnings call , Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler mentioned that lower monetization within AI Mode was one of three reasons for the slower growth.

In addition to announcing expanded availability of ads in AI Mode in ten additional markets, Alphabet also stated that it is launching ads in AI Mode follow-on question functionality in the United States. All existing Search, Shopping, and Performance Max campaigns are eligible by default and cannot opt out separately.

The biggest factor driving the search slow down compared to Q2 was, according to Schindler, currency movements. Retail also experienced an impact, he said, with certain Asia-Pacific advertisers affected by the E.U. eliminating its de minimis exemption for low-value imports. Media and entertainment saw spending normalize after a strong Q2 which included the FIFA World Cup.

Google CFO Anat Ashkenazi stated that currency movement was a small headwind to the year over year growth and a larger headwind to the quarter over quarter growth. Ashkenazi also mentioned that there was a tougher compare because the search growth continued to accelerate throughout the second half of 2025.

On the Q2 earnings conference call in July, Ashkenazi had signaled both items stating that Google expected a slight FX headwind in Q3 primarily in Search & YouTube ads. Additionally, she stated that search would begin lapping last year’s acceleration in Q3.

In my prior report I noted in July that Q2 was the first time we had seen a slow down in search growth after 4 quarters of accelerating growth. The issue at hand then was if it was a temporary slow down or if it represented the beginning of a period of slowing growth.

Related : Google’s Ads Decoded Explores How AI Is Changing Search Behavior

What Google Said About AI Mode Monetization

CEO Sundar Pichai stated during the earnings announcement that AI investment has driven Search query growth (including commercial queries) as well as the “year-over-year query growth rate is the highest it’s been in the last five years.”

During the call with investors, J.P. Morgan analyst Doug Anmuth questioned the difference in year over year query growth and Search ad revenue growth. Schindler noted it was currency, retail and media first and then stated that strong AI mode query growth negatively impacted search revenue growth due to lower monetization in AI Mode. He did not state what AI mode’s monetization was lower than, nor the amount of money this impacted search ad revenue.

“Just like our shift to mobile over a decade ago, we are focused on building the best Search user experience, followed by monetization.”

In his prepared remarks, Schindler said many of the new questions people ask in AI-powered Search are upper-funnel, and that the majority of AI Mode queries are incremental, which he said creates more monetization opportunities over time.

In Google’s announcement post, Shashi Thakur, VP and GM of Google Search Ads and Ads on Google Experiences, wrote:

“Our research shows that people are comfortable with ads in AI Mode and find them highly relevant. In fact, click-through rates are already similar between sponsored and organic product list items within AI Mode.”

A footnote references a source of Google’s click through comparison, which is internal data for Google in the United States for the time period August 20th thru September 3rd of 2026.

At the Google Marketing Live event in May of 2025, Thakur stated to reporters, including me, that AI Overviews generate revenue “at the same rate” as those exact searches when there are no overviews. This claim covered AI Overviews, but does not include data on AI mode.

Google is scaling ads in AI Mode in Australia, Canada, India, Kenya, Malaysia, New Zealand, Nigeria, Pakistan, the Philippines, and Singapore.

articles.title: How to Teach Content Strategy to Stakeholders Who Don’t Speak Marketing
articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Content strategy buy-in often breaks down in translation to non-marketers, even when the strategy is sound.  
  • Lead with what your stakeholder already measures. How a strategy ties back to organizational cost, risk, or speed means more to them than marketing buzzwords. 
  • Call attention to problems or poor performance yourself. Clarify any wrong conclusions and present solutions before stakeholders have time to spiral. 
  • Name what stays the same before you name what changes, so new tactics feel familiar to your audience. 
  • General recommendations rarely get implemented. Give your audience specific action items in a portable checklist or one-pager. 

Most content strategies don’t fail on their merits. They stall out because content strategy buy-in never arrives from the person who funds the work, approves it, or executes part of it. That might be a client-side VP, your own executive team, a sales director, or a legal reviewer who has never opened your editorial calendar. 

The data supports the gap. Content Marketing Institute research ranks cross-department collaboration among the top content marketing challenges for 21 percent of B2B marketers. 

Content marketers get very good at doing the work but still struggle to convince stakeholders how necessary it is. Those are separate skills, and we need plenty of practice in both. 

If you feel like you’re failing to get the right stakeholders on side for your strategy, read on. You’ll learn how to explain content strategy to non-marketers, so they understand the rationale enough to defend it (even when you aren’t in the room). 

Teaching Is a Different Skill Than Doing

When stakeholders deny or ignore content strategy, we usually blame the audience. Leadership doesn’t get it. The client won’t listen. Sales ignored the brief (again). 

That explanation feels comfortable, but it’s not always the truth. The question is, how well are we explaining ourselves? 

The same pattern shows up in every department. A client executive, a product manager, and a compliance reviewer all evaluate your recommendation against a different set of priorities. A decision that looks obvious to a content strategist can read as a cost or a liability to someone who only thinks about content for 20 minutes a month. 

Stakeholder education in content marketing is a learnable skill, not a personality trait. Nobody is born knowing how to translate a content audit into CFO speak. You practice, watch what explanations tend to land, and adjust. Here’s what I’ve found works consistently. 

Start with the Stakes, Not the Solution

Lead with why the decision matters to the specific person in front of you, in their terms, before you name a framework or tactic. This does more for getting buy-in for content strategy than any deck you build. 

Attention follows relevance. Open with a scenario that matches your stakeholder’s priorities, then connect your recommendation to it. 

Use this same move across different audiences: 

  • A budget holder hears a content refresh as spend on something already done. Reframe it as efficiency. You’re reinvesting in assets that already earn traffic instead of funding net-new pages that take months to mature.  
  • Legal hears a byline requirement on articles as more review work eating up their time. Reframe it as attribution control. Named authors with verifiable credentials reduce the risk of unsourced claims attributed to the company. 
  • Sales hears a webpage restructure as a cosmetic change. Reframe it as speed. Clear subheads and direct answers let a rep send one link mid-deal instead of writing a custom explanation. 

Translate your content strategy into the currency your audience already trades in, then explain the specifics where you need sign-off. Most collaborators tune in if you’re covering cost, risk, or speed. 

Beyond buzzwords, root your argument in data they recognize. A content strategist lives in organic sessions, keyword rankings, and time on page. A sales leader watches pipeline contribution and deal velocity; a CFO watches customer acquisition cost and ROI. You don’t have to drop your own metrics, just connect them. Bring the organic sessions that became pipeline; tie your rankings to the deals they influenced. Pull evidence from the dashboard they already open, then draw the line from your metric to theirs. 

Defuse the Scariest Interpretation Before They Invent It

Nearly every content strategy shift arrives attached to an alarming headline. A traffic decline. A ranking drop. A platform change nobody controls. 

The Pew Research Center tracked 68,879 Google searches and found click-through fell from 15% to 8% when an AI Overview appeared. Read that insight cold in a quarterly review and your client hears one message: our investment is evaporating. 

Speak to those concerns before they raise them. State the numbers plainly, then correct potential wrong conclusions immediately. Something like this works: “organic clicks are getting harder to win on informational queries as search engine trends shift, which is why we’re moving effort toward pages that convert and toward becoming the source these systems cite.” 

Skipping an uncomfortable number doesn’t make it disappear. Your audience fills in the blank themselves, usually with something worse than reality, and you find out during Q&A after you’ve lost the floor. ...

For brands, social media is a goldmine of real-time insight into consumers’ preferences, behaviors and motivations. And segmenting social users intentionally—using live conversation data rather than static demographic details—empowers leaders to make smarter business decisions, whether it’s optimizing spend, discovering new markets or driving revenue.

But social media audience segmentation isn’t a one‑off marketing exercise. It’s a dynamic, cyclical process designed to spot emerging opportunities and inform data-grounded strategies.

With the help of this guide, you can better understand how to approach social media audience segmentation and use it to make an impact across the business.

What is social media audience segmentation?

Social media audience segmentation is the process of breaking down your target audience that’s engaging on social networks into smaller, distinct groups based on shared characteristics, behaviors or interests.

In contrast to broader marketing segmentation, social segmentation draws on real-time social data. Think live conversation, engagement and sentiment data, rather than CRM or survey inputs that may reflect the past and not a user’s present feelings.

Segmentation is one of the many pillars of social media intelligence, helping organizations move beyond broad audience assumptions by uncovering the distinct groups driving conversations online. Teams can then make more targeted decisions aligned to the current pulse of the market across customer care, product innovation, campaign planning and overall business strategy.

Why audience segmentation matters more than ever

One of the key factors driving the need for segmentation is the degradation of trust and attention among consumers.

According to the Q1 2026 Sprout Pulse Survey, consumers are becoming more particular about what they engage with online, with two-thirds (66%) feeling more selective than a year ago. AI slop (i.e. undifferentiated, one-size-fits-all content) was cited as a contributor to eroding trust; 56% of respondents said they see AI slop often or very often.

Many brands are mistakenly investing in this generic content. This ultimately results in wasted budget as platforms are increasingly rewarding relevance over reach.

Segmentation is what enables brands to achieve personalization and, in turn, resonance with their audiences—without necessarily needing to increase headcount or budget.

4 types of social media audience segments (and where social data fits)

Let’s take a look at four key types of social media audience segments, what they tell you and the social signals that paint the picture of who they are.

Demographic segmentation

Basic demographics like age, gender or follower count are a reasonable starting point in creating social media segments. This data is garnered via self-disclosure (i.e. a user inputs this information when creating a profile), network-level audience demographics reported by ad managers or analytics tools.

While these details don’t tell you much on their own, they can reveal behavioral trends. For instance, you may see a generational skew depending on the networks and content formats a person engages with. In general, Instagram Reels and TikToks attract a younger audience, while Facebook’s most active users skew older.

However, it’s important to note that demographics don’t provide the soundest basis for segmentation because the data is often self-reported. Users may skip fields or deliberately enter false details to protect their privacy or access age-restricted content.

Demographic-based targeting is also losing its predictive power. Per the 2026 Influencer Marketing Report, only 17% of consumers check follower count before following a creator. For nearly half of respondents (47%), things like content topic and behavior matter far more.

With that in mind, demographics should be used as a starting point rather than a primary segmentation driver. Instead of examining people’s surface-level traits, look at the things they say and do unprompted on social. These signals are more dynamic and indicative of how people identify themselves.

Psychographic segmentation

Psychographics is the classification of people based on psychological criteria—such as values, attitudes or motivations—that influence their engagement and consumption patterns.

To segment your social audience by psychographics, review their comments, posts and shares. The content they post or engage with can tell you a lot about their internal beliefs. Your brand can then use these insights to tailor its content and target these users more closely.

For example, if your audience members regularly post about climate change and sustainability, you can place them into an environmentally motivated segment. From there, you can center your messaging around subjects related to your brand, like ethically sourced materials, reusable products or community initiatives.

Behavioral segmentation on social

While psychographics focus on what users believe, behavioral segmentation shines a light on how they behave on social. The actions they take, the conversations they partake in and the content formats they engage with.

To build behavioral segments, brands must observe audiences’ patterns. How often do they post? What formats do they share (e.g. static images, carousels, Reels)? What are they talking about in comment sections? Whose posts are they commenting on?

Finding the answers to these questions can unearth important information about consumers’ decision-making and motivations. In addition to seeing how people behave, you’ll begin to understand why. You won’t just see who they interact with, but who they really are behind the screen.

Say you identify a segment of users consistently participating in giveaways, promo codes and engaging with shopping-on-a-budget content. With this data, you can glean what might be most important to them when making purchase decisions: fair pricing and discount offers. From there, you can tailor your social messaging accordingly, whether it’s highlighting affordable prices or sharing the outsized value of your offerings.

Geographic segmentation

A person’s physical location shapes their social and spending habits—and the two often go hand in hand.

Various social signals enable brands to glean a user’s whereabouts, including location tags, geotagged posts and stories, and the language or dialect they use on social. Additionally, some network behaviors and preferences are region-specific.

articles.title: Social media leadership skills for 2026 (+ KPIs to track)
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. Social media leadership skills combine strategic thinking, emotional intelligence, AI fluency, and cross-functional communication to guide enterprise teams toward business outcomes.
  2. The biggest shift in 2026 is leading AI adoption responsibly, balancing speed and governance without losing the human element.
  3. Strong social leaders measure success through team health, brand reputation, and business impact, not vanity metrics.
  4. Developing social media leadership skills requires structured feedback, clear decision-making frameworks, and a willingness to experiment and fail fast.

What are social media leadership skills?

Social media leadership skills are a blend of abilities, both learned and innate, that help leaders direct and inspire social media teams to succeed. They matter at every scale, but they matter most in enterprise environments where one decision can ripple across dozens of markets.

The core skills include:

  • Strategic thinking: Connecting social activity to business goals like revenue, retention, and reputation, rather than treating channels as standalone projects.
  • Emotional intelligence: Reading the room internally and externally, spotting burnout early, and handling sensitive moments without defensiveness.
  • Communication aptitude: Explaining social performance in language the C-suite, legal, and frontline teams all understand.
  • AI fluency: Knowing which tasks to hand to AI, which to keep human, and how to govern the output.
  • Adaptability: Shifting plans quickly when platforms, policies, or culture change without losing the thread of the strategy.
  • Creativity and innovative thinking: Creating room for teams to test new formats, including the ones that look strange on a slide.
  • Collaboration and conflict management: Navigating competing stakeholder priorities and saying no when the request does not serve the strategy.

A successful social media leader’s skills must go beyond social media management. A true leader understands how to delegate and guide in real time through an evolving industry and culture. They know how to use a social strategy to achieve business goals.

It’s no surprise, then, that a recent IBM study found 69% of CEO respondents say their organization’s success is directly tied to maintaining a broad group of leaders with a deep understanding of strategy and the authority to make critical decisions. Social is no exception.

Shakivla Todd, a 4-time Shorty award-winning Social Media Strategist, says a great social leader must be “naturally culturally aware and in-the-know.”

“You don’t need to be chronically online. But you do need to be acutely aware of what’s happening as it pertains to current events and cultural moments.”

Cultural relevance isn’t just to stay ‘on trend,’ says Todd. It’s to “help lead your team through culturally sensitive moments. An exceptional social media leader should know how to read the damn room, everyone hates a tone-deaf brand.”

In short: social media leadership skills are the mix of strategic, human, and technical abilities that turn a capable social team into a business function executives rely on.

How is social media leadership different from management?

Social media leadership sets the direction; social media management executes against it. Both roles are essential, and most leaders have done both, but the day-to-day work looks very different.

Social media managers focus on executing a social media strategy. Their social tasks include:

  • Creating and publishing compelling content
  • Understanding how social networks like LinkedIn, TikTok, or Instagram work
  • Engaging an audience
  • Analyzing and optimizing performance
  • Maintaining brand voice

Social media leaders, on the other hand, set a direction and keep everyone working toward it. They:

  • Shape the long-term vision
  • Advocate for resources
  • Build systems that allow their teams to move quickly while staying aligned

A manager might be optimizing a campaign’s engagement rate. A leader is the one asking how that engagement ladders up to revenue, reputation, and retention.

In social, business leaders have to stay flexible. The industry changes fast, and you need to be able to pivot, using new trends and real data, to build initiatives that actually move the business forward.

“Keeping up with the swiftness of social media is an Olympic sport,” says Todd. “I’ve learned to be comfortable with uncertainty, and I don’t get too attached to plans.”

What does a social media director do?

A social media director sits between management and leadership, owning the strategic direction of social while staying close enough to the work to guide it. The role is usually where social media leadership skills get tested for the first time at scale.

Typical social media director responsibilities include:

  • Strategy ownership: Setting the annual social strategy and making sure every channel maps to a business objective.
  • Team oversight: Hiring, structuring, and developing the social team, including agency and freelance partners.
  • Budget and resourcing: Building the business case for headcount, tools, and paid support.
  • Executive reporting: Translating social performance into the metrics leadership already tracks.

articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. Instagram Reels deliver higher reach and engagement than other Instagram post types, which makes them the most effective format for business visibility in 2026.
  2. The Reels algorithm prioritizes watch time and completion rate, plus shares and saves, so hooking viewers in the first 1-2 seconds matters most.
  3. Mixing trending formats with evergreen content like tutorials, behind-the-scenes clips, and product demos builds short-term reach and long-term audience growth.
  4. Scheduling Reels at optimal times and tracking performance metrics helps teams refine strategy and prove ROI.

What is an Instagram Reel?

An Instagram Reel is a short-form vertical video shared on Instagram. You can record, edit, and stitch multiple video clips and photos together, then add extras like:

  • Original audio or trending sounds
  • Voiceovers
  • Text overlays and stickers
  • Effects and transitions

Reels and TikToks are both short-form video platforms, but they differ in audience, reach, content style, and more.

Here’s a breakdown of the main differences between a Reel and a TikTok:

How long can Instagram Reels be?

Reels can be up to 3 minutes long. That change took effect in January 2025, raising the limit from the previous 90 seconds.

That said, just because you can post longer videos doesn’t mean you should. According to Adam Mosseri, Head of Instagram, when it comes to Reels, the shorter the better.

Check out his Reel below on the ideal Reel length:

Source: Adam Mosseri

What video sizes and specs work best for Instagram Reels?

The best Instagram Reels size is 1080 x 1920 pixels with a 9:16 aspect ratio. Because Reels are designed for full-screen mobile viewing, vertical videos perform best.

Here are the recommended Instagram Reels specs:

  • Aspect ratio: Between 1.91:1 and 9:16
  • Resolution: 1080 × 1920 pixels recommended (minimum 720p)
  • Frame rate: Minimum of 30 frames per second (FPS)

Why use Instagram Reels for business?

Instagram Reels are worth the investment because they reach people who don’t follow you yet across a platform where half of U.S. adults are active, which is hard to do with any other post type. Instagram has said that through its recommendations, creators of all sizes have an equal chance of breaking through and reaching new audiences, and Reels are the format that recommendation engine favors.

Here’s what that means for a business account:

  • Reach beyond your followers: Reels surface in the Reels feed and on Explore, so a single video can introduce your brand to people who have never heard of you.
  • Higher engagement: Reels tend to earn more interactions per post than static images or carousels, largely because saves, shares, and rewatches all count. Use an engagement rate calculator to benchmark yours.
  • Discoverability through search and audio: Search-friendly captions, on-screen text, and sounds all give Instagram more context to match your video with interested viewers.
  • Commerce built in: Product tagging lets viewers tap straight from a Reel to a product page, shortening the path from discovery to purchase.
  • Trust and authenticity: Faces, voices, and unpolished moments give audiences a sense of who’s behind the brand in a way a product photo can’t.

In short, Reels are the most efficient way to buy attention on Instagram without paying for it, which is why they belong in almost every brand’s social media strategy.

  • The 4 Ps (product, price, place, and promotion) are tools marketers use in combination to shape how a product (or range of products) is positioned, promoted, and sold to a specific group of customers. Together, they’re often referred to as the “marketing mix.”

The 4 Ps of marketing (product, price, place, and promotion) have been around for decades, and they still drive decisions around every successful product launch.

Also known as the “marketing mix,” they help you think through how to bring a product to market and reach the customers most likely to buy it.

It doesn’t matter if you’re running a one-person small business or a global enterprise. The 4 Ps help you bring a product to market and get it in front of people most likely to buy it.

How you put the 4 Ps to work has changed, though. AI is giving marketers new ways to understand their customers and make more informed decisions, often in less time.

I’ll cover some of these opportunities as I show you how the 4 Ps still drive marketing decision-making today.

What Are the Four Elements of the Marketing Mix?

The 4 Ps of marketing, commonly known as the marketing mix, stand for product, place, price, and promotion. They’re like four levers companies can adjust to better position their products for the customers they want to reach.

Here’s the meaning behind each of the four Ps: 

  • Product: What you’re selling, including its features, packaging, and the support that comes with it
  • Price: What you charge and how you structure the pricing
  • Place: Where and how your customers can buy the product
  • Promotion: How you get the word out about the product

To more fully understand the 4 Ps of advertising, we need to take a step back. Mention “marketing,” and most people think of customer-facing content like ads, social media posts, emails, videos, and blog articles like this one. 

In fact, these represent just one piece of a much broader discipline. They’re the “promotion” part of the mix called marketing communications.

True marketing is a big-picture process that strives to meet all customer needs. And thinking in terms of the 4 Ps allows companies to do exactly that. 

What About the 7 Ps and the 4 Cs?

The idea of a marketing mix has been around longer than the 4 Ps themselves.

In 1948, Harvard professor James Culliton described marketing executives as “mixer(s) of ingredients.” Inspired by this idea, fellow Harvard professor Neil Borden often referred to the concept of the marketing mix in the years that followed. 

Then in 1960, marketing professor E. Jerome McCarthy organized it into the four elements we know today in his book Basic Marketing: A Managerial Approach.

Other models have been suggested in the years since, with two in particular gaining traction: the 7 Ps and the 4 Cs:

Their model adds people, process, and physical evidence to the mix. These cover the employees who deliver a service, the delivery process, and the environment where business takes place. 
  • The 4 Cs: Marketing professor Robert Lauterborn proposed a more customer-oriented alternative to the 4 Ps in 1990. His model replaces them with consumer wants and needs, cost, convenience, and communication. Instead of starting with what a business wants to sell, the 4 Cs push marketers to focus on what customers actually need.

A social media dashboard is a single interface that pulls metrics from all your social accounts into one place for tracking, analyzing, and reporting on performance.

Enterprise marketing teams, agencies managing multiple clients, and growing social teams rely on them most, because the reporting burden scales with every new account and campaign.

Instead of logging into Instagram, LinkedIn, Facebook, TikTok, and X separately to check results, a dashboard brings everything together. You get a single view of what’s working, what’s not, and how your social efforts connect to business goals.

Dashboards tend to fall into four categories, and knowing which one you’re building keeps you from cramming every metric into a single view. The four types are operational, analytical, strategic, and tactical.

  • Analytical: Deeper performance analysis across longer time ranges, used to find patterns in content, formats, and audiences.

Real-time decision-making

articles.title: How to build your social media team for the future of marketing
articles.fullContent:
It’s certainly not 2010 anymore. So why are so many businesses still resourcing social media teams as if it is?

Social teams have evolved far beyond publishing posts and responding to comments. Today, they manage content and video production, influencer partnerships, customer care, social search, paid media, community engagement and increasingly, social intelligence. Social’s role is expanding across the business, and a social team’s structure needs to evolve with it.

Organizations are also looking to social data for more than marketing insights. According to Sprout’s Social Intelligence Report, 93% of leaders view social intelligence as essential for future growth, yet only 10% of organizations have embedded it into enterprise strategy. Closing that gap requires more support for social teams that are already stretched across a growing list of responsibilities. They need the right people, roles and processes to turn social data into action across the business while creating more capacity for strategic work.

There’s no one-size-fits-all social media team structure. But the strongest teams connect their work directly to business outcomes rather than organizing solely around the tasks they complete. Building for that future requires the right mix of specialized expertise, cross-functional relationships and technology to keep pace with social’s expanding role.

In this guide, we’ll break down how to structure a social media team, which roles to prioritize and how to build and manage a team that’s prepared for the future of marketing.

How to structure a social media team

Social’s dynamic nature can give marketers a professional advantage if leaders give them space to grow. With the right structure, teams can quickly refine and grow their skills, creating career-making opportunities.

Proactively experimenting with new social media department structures can also shift a brand’s trajectory—helping it win a larger audience, build customer loyalty and sustain growth.

Here are four common models to consider, plus how your structure may evolve as your company grows.

1. Functional

The functional model organizes social media team roles around specific responsibilities, such as influencer partnerships, social media intelligence or paid media. Generalists may also have defined focus areas, including content creation, video production and social search optimization (SOSEO).

At Sprout, the social team also partners closely with Brand Creative on asset development and with teams across the organization—including PR, Content, Customer Marketing, Events, Internal Comms, Revenue Marketing and Product Marketing—on messaging, research and distribution.

Constantly switching between incoming DMs, reporting, influencer coordination and content production can limit time for creative and strategic thinking. A functional structure can help reduce burnout, clarify ownership and create more room for social marketers to deepen their expertise.

With clearer focus areas, teams can scale priority initiatives and measure their impact more effectively. This model works especially well for organizations that want to support career development while assigning clear ownership to specific social priorities.

2. Network

Some teams align individual employees to specific networks, such as TikTok, Instagram, Facebook or LinkedIn. With this approach, each person owns a network strategy from development through execution, which in turn enables them to build deep network expertise.

Sprout’s social team experimented with a network-specific structure in 2022 before eventually moving away from it. While the model supported highly intentional content and stronger network-specific audience insights, it wasn’t scalable for a growing team.

The social landscape has also become more fluid since network-based structures first gained popularity. New networks emerge and consumer preferences change rapidly, creating gaps or redundancies when roles are tied too closely to individual networks.

A network-based social structure can still work as an interim model for lean teams developing their social media marketing strategy from the ground up. As the team grows, shifting toward functional ownership can make it easier to adapt across networks.

3. Audience engagement

Another common team structure organizes social media team roles around audience engagement goals and customer needs. These typically fall into three categories:

  • Awareness: Creating content to increase brand visibility among new and existing audiences.
  • Engagement: Creating content and responding to comments, DMs and other inbound interactions to build community and strengthen brand loyalty.
  • Customer Service: Managing customer questions, requests and complaints to resolve issues quickly.

These teams often include specialists beyond content and community management. For example, an awareness-focused team might include a content creator, an influencer marketing strategist and a performance analyst who work together to develop relevant and effective content.

Because this model requires employees to work across multiple networks, centralized social media management software becomes especially important. Bringing publishing, engagement, reporting and collaboration into one system reduces time spent switching between disconnected platforms.

4. Center of excellence

In a social media center of excellence (CoE) model, representatives from different departments form a central council that shapes social strategy and establishes shared standards.

Participants may include leaders from PR, employer brand, HR, product, customer care and other teams that rely on or contribute to social. Together, they align priorities, improve information sharing and create clearer governance around how the organization uses social.

CoE models tend to work best for large organizations with social stakeholders spread across multiple departments or regions. A centralized group reduces silos and gives distributed teams a shared framework for decision-making, measurement and execution.

5. Structure by company size

Company size can help determine which structure makes the most sense, but complexity is often the better signal. A lean team may work well with broad ownership until the volume of channels, stakeholders and social data becomes difficult for a few people to manage.

As demand grows, teams usually need more specialization and clearer ownership. Enterprise organizations also need stronger governance, especially when social intelligence spans multiple departments.   3. Set your baselines: Record where each metric sits before the program launches (or before your next big push). Without a baseline, you have numbers but no story.
  4. Agree on a reporting cadence: Review participation and engagement monthly so you can course-correct quickly. Save business impact metrics like pipeline and earned media value for quarterly reviews.

What is an employee advocacy program?

An employee advocacy program is a structured initiative that encourages employees to share company-approved content on their personal social media accounts to extend brand reach and build trust.

It’s a powerful part of any social media marketing and content strategy. Instead of relying only on your brand’s accounts to do the talking, employees post about your company on platforms like LinkedIn, X, or wherever they’re already active.

Sometimes that content is promotional, like a new campaign, product launch, or company milestone. Other times it’s cultural, offering a peek into what it’s actually like to work at your company.

The reason it works is simple: people trust other people more than they trust corporations. In fact, 88% of consumers say trusting a brand is an important or critical purchase criterion, on par with quality and value, according to Edelman.

When your employees share authentic stories, it humanizes your brand, boosts your organic reach, and helps you connect with your target audience in ways standard corporate messaging just can’t.

Successful employee advocacy programs are built on:

  • Clear marketing goals
  • Measurable KPIs to track performance
  • Easy-to-share content and guidelines for employees

The benefits for the company are wide-reaching:

  • Increased brand awareness,
  • Improved reputation,
  • Boosted engagement, and
  • Talent recruitment, to name a few.

In short, every employee share strengthens both your internal company culture and your external trust, turning your team into your most credible marketing channel.

Informal advocacy vs. structured programs: what’s the difference?

The difference between informal advocacy and a structured program comes down to intention.

  • Informal advocacy: Spontaneous and personal. Genuine, but unpredictable. You can’t count on it, measure it, or repeat it.
  • Structured programs: Intentional, consistent, and built to scale, because employees get the tools, content, and guidelines they need to share regularly.

Most successful employee advocacy programs include:

  • Curated content hubs: Where employees can access pre-approved content
  • Training and resources: To help staff build their personal brand while staying on-message
  • Incentives or recognition: That encourage ongoing participation
  • Measurement and analytics: To track reach, engagement, and business impact

Employees get a curated feed of pre-approved content they can post in a few taps, while admins measure performance across every share, gamify participation with leaderboards, and keep posts aligned with brand and legal guidelines.

Why do companies invest in employee advocacy programs?

Companies invest in employee advocacy programs because they drive real business outcomes: wider reach, stronger reputation, better recruitment, and more pipeline, all at a fraction of the cost of traditional marketing.

To understand what this looks like in practice, we chatted with Victoria Samways, Marketing & Brand Manager at Major Tom, and a long-time user of Hootsuite’s employee advocacy tools.

“Our employees are very powerful brand ambassadors,” says Samways. “Each employee can easily have hundreds of connections on LinkedIn alone. Multiply that by the number of employees a brand has, and that’s a large audience.“

  2. Stronger talent attraction and recruiting
  3. Improved brand reputation and trust
  4. Higher organic engagement
  5. Sales pipeline and lead generation
  6. Career and personal brand benefits for employees

1. Expanded brand reach and awareness

Collectively, employees have a wide social reach. Tapping into your employees’ networks is one of the easiest ways to reach new audiences without spending a dollar on paid media. And it also feels more authentic.

The math is straightforward. A company of 500 employees with 500 LinkedIn connections each has access to a potential audience of 250,000 people, most of whom will never follow the brand page. That’s why brand reach is usually the first metric advocacy programs move.

2. Stronger talent attraction and recruiting

A careers page can promise great culture all day long, but a real employee sharing what it’s actually like to work there? That’s way more convincing.

When teams post authentically about their work (wins, projects, team moments, or even just what a typical day looks like), it offers a genuine peek at the employee experience.

Partner with influencers to create tailored content for specific demographics. From fashion lovers to tech enthusiasts, influencers can connect with high-intent niche audiences. Offering special discounts and promo codes via influencers is one way to track ROI of a campaign and boost sales. In fact, promo codes are the leading factor influencing the purchasing decisions of social media scrollers. Thirty percent of respondents to the Q3 pulse survey said promo codes influencers share make them more likely to purchase from a brand during the holidays, more than any other factor in the survey.

Working with influencers who can create hyper-relevant content is key to getting your campaign seen by new audiences. Small businesses with modest budgets and larger companies alike can embrace micro-influencer marketing this gifting season.

AI is changing more than how quickly marketers can create content. It is changing how marketing teams operate.

McKinsey’s latest research argues that AI is moving organizations away from campaign-based marketing and toward continuous growth, supported by capabilities such as hyperpersonalization, scaled creativity, and AI-native discoverability. That shift has important implications for content teams, particularly as AI changes how audiences discover and evaluate information.

The opportunity isn’t simply to produce more content with AI. Brands need systems that connect audience insights, human expertise, content creation, distribution, and performance measurement. The teams that build these processes can continuously improve their content while adapting to changing audience behavior and search environments.

AI Is Changing How Marketing Operates

McKinsey’s research points to a broader change in marketing: AI is moving teams away from isolated campaigns and toward a continuously improving growth engine.

The common thread is that these capabilities work together rather than operating as separate AI experiments.

Traditional campaigns are usually planned around a defined launch, run for a set period, and evaluated afterward.

McKinsey argues that the campaign-era marketing model is becoming less effective as customer behavior changes. Its research found that while many organizations are experimenting with AI, fewer than 10% have scaled it or captured value across marketing workflows.

This is why content operations are becoming increasingly important.

Your visual identity is often the first interaction a potential customer has with your brand. A strong visual strategy makes that first impression count and getting your dimensions right is where it starts.

Why do social media image sizes matter?

Social media image sizes are the pixel dimensions, aspect ratios and file limits each platform uses to display profile photos, cover images and posts. Match them and your visuals stay sharp and uncropped.

Miss them and the platform makes the call for you. Wrong sizes signal to your audience that your brand doesn’t sweat the details. Here’s what happens:

  • Compression: Fine detail turns soft and blurry
  • Letterboxing: Mismatched ratios leave empty space around your image

Scheduling tools publish through platform APIs, which enforce stricter limits than the apps. Instagram’s API, for example, accepts feed images between 4:5 and 1.91:1 and nothing outside that range.

articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Websites remain an important way for consumers to verify that a business is legitimate.
  • Wix’s State of Websites report found that search still accounts for 42% of website traffic.
  • Sites with structured data that passes Google’s rich-results inspection earn 2x more revenue and 9x more traffic than sites without it.
  • Blogs and reviews can strengthen a brand’s authority and contribute to business growth.
  • As AI changes discovery, a credible website can give consumers and AI systems a reliable source of information about a brand.

AI has made it easier than ever to create a website, generate content, and put a brand online. That speed comes with a new challenge: consumers have more reason to question what they see.

A convincing business can appear online almost overnight. For customers, a website therefore has an important job beyond selling products or services. It can help establish that a business is real.

Wix’s first State of Websites report, based on data from more than 300 million users, examines how websites are being built, discovered, and used in the age of AI. The report found that websites remain central to business growth, even as discovery expands across AI platforms and other channels.

For marketers, the takeaway is straightforward. Website credibility still matters. The challenge is making sure a website provides the information, content, and technical signals that support trust with both people and machines.

Why Websites Still Matter in the Age of AI

AI search is changing how people find information, but it hasn’t eliminated the need for a destination where customers can verify what they’ve learned.

Source

Websites Help Consumers Verify a Business

Wix’s research describes a growing tension around AI and website creation. Building a site is becoming faster, but customers still need confidence that a business is legitimate.

That makes a website part of the validation process.

Structured data gives machines additional context about the information presented on a page. As search experiences become more sophisticated, that machine-readable layer can help make important information easier to interpret.

Authenticity is the most important brand characteristic on social media, according to Sprout’s Q3 2026 Pulse Survey. But as audiences grow more skeptical of what they see in their feeds, brands need to work harder to earn their trust.

People rely on social media for news, product recommendations and connection. At the same time, Sprout’s Q1 2026 Pulse Survey found that 35% of users trust social media less than they did a year ago. AI-generated content adds to that skepticism, making it harder to distinguish real experiences from manufactured ones.

Sprout’s Be So FR webinar explored this “trust recession” and the growing demand for content that reflects real people and experiences. Brands need to show who’s behind their content and follow through when customers reach out.

Building trust through social media starts with what you publish and how you respond to your audience. In this guide, we’ll explore what earns audience trust and practical ways to strengthen it.

Why trust is now built on social media first

People often encounter your brand through someone else’s post before they visit your website. They search for recommendations, compare customer experiences and ask questions in the comments. Those interactions help them decide whether to trust you.

Sprout’s 2026 Pulse Surveys show how people use social to find information and decide what to buy:

  • Search: 21% of consumers turn to social media first when searching for information, according to Q2 data.
  • Influencer impact: 67% made a purchase directly because of an influencer’s recommendation in the past year.
  • Trends and culture: Q3 data found that 54% of consumers turn to social media to keep up with trends and cultural moments, ahead of TV and streaming at 45% and conversations with friends and family at 42%.

These social media statistics show why brands need to pay attention to conversations beyond their own accounts. With influencers playing such a significant role in what people buy, choosing credible partners matters.

For example, viewers of @theglownarrative’s skincare review discuss product prices, share what they want to try and recommend alternatives. Her review gives viewers a starting point, while the comments offer additional perspectives. Brands that partner with creators who share honest, firsthand experiences give potential customers more reason to trust their products.


The same online scrutiny applies when something goes wrong for a brand too. According to Sprout’s Q2 2026 Pulse Survey, consumers first hear about a brand crisis on social. And 64% say it’s important for brands to respond publicly on social rather than through a press release or website statement.

How building trust on social media is a growth lever

Social media’s influence gives brands a chance to turn audience trust into growth. When people trust your brand, they’re more likely to choose your products and recommend them to others. As Sprout’s Q2 2026 Pulse Survey highlights, creating multiple points of connection with your brand and through partnerships with trusted voices can strengthen customer relationships and support growth:

  • Authentic influencer partnerships build buying confidence. Eighty-one percent of consumers say it matters whether an influencer has used the product they promote. Creators with firsthand product experience offer more credible recommendations.
  • Employee content introduces potential customers to your business. Forty percent of consumers rated employee-generated content as more authentic than posts from a brand’s main account. The same proportion discover products or services through employee content at least once a month.
  • Timely crisis responses protect customer relationships. Response speed influences how consumers judge a brand’s public crisis response. Addressing problems promptly and following through on a solution gives customers a reason to keep doing business with you.

A consistent voice and posting cadence set expectations for your brand. Your values need the same follow-through: if you promote a commitment to customer care, your replies should reflect it. Maintain that reliability across everyday posts, campaigns and difficult conversations.

Speed matters during crises, too, as Q2 pulse survey findings show. Acknowledge the issue promptly, explain what you know and tell people when to expect an update. The quality of your response matters as much as how quickly you send it.

Transparency

Be up front about how you create your content and what you’re promoting. That includes paid partnerships, relevant AI use and the limits of your product claims.

articles.fullContent:
You’ve heard it from mentors, recruiters and that coworker who posts on LinkedIn every morning: You need a personal brand. Truth is, you already have one, because people form a public perception of your brand whether you shape it or not. This guide shows you how to take control of that perception and turn it into real opportunities.

Personal branding once sounded like a celebrity-only game. Today, founders, marketers, job seekers and employees use it to stand out in crowded feeds and earn trust before they ever say hello. It’s how people decide whether to follow you, hire you or buy from you.

Branding yourself feels daunting when you don’t know where to start. But the strongest personal brands are built on who you already are.

You don’t need a massive following, a big budget or a magnetic personality. You need well-defined goals, a sharp sense of your value and the habit of showing up.

Ready to build yours? Let’s dig in.

What is personal branding?

Personal branding is how you present yourself as an individual to your audience. It’s the mix of expertise, values and personality people associate with your name. Our glossary definition covers the short version, and this guide shows you how to build one.

The idea isn’t new. Management writer Tom Peters popularized it in 1997 with his Fast Company essay “The Brand Called You.” Social media turned his idea into something anyone with a phone can act on.

Think about how corporate branding works. We associate specific feelings, values and expectations with brands we trust. Every company has a story and image.

The same applies to you and your personal brand. The difference comes down to who owns it, how it sounds and what it’s for.

People often treat personal branding as a synonym for being an influencer. It doesn’t have to be. A software engineer, a nurse and a small business owner can each build a personal brand without chasing fame.

Your brand should highlight your human side. Voices and personalities set brands (and people!) apart. Branding yourself means aligning your online persona with your real-life one.

Building your brand goes beyond just marketing yourself. Here are the key pieces of a personal brand:

  • Voice and values. That is, what you say and what you believe. Your brand voice shouldn’t be one-size-fits-all or robotic.

  • Content. What you create, and how you present it, attracts your audience. If you write long-form newsletters, mastering Substack SEO gets those deep dives discovered by new readers.

  • Creativity. You don’t need to be a creative genius to build a personal brand. But some sort of creative trademark helps you stand out from the crowd.

  • Personality. There’s no one-size-fits-all personality type for your brand. Energetic, laid back or suit-and-tie, you do you.

  • Authenticity. Your personal brand shouldn’t feel manufactured or made up. Align your online persona with who you are offline and your brand will never feel forced.

Why is personal branding important?

Here is why building a personal brand is worth the effort.

Standing out from the crowd

The people who’d benefit the most from a personal brand are often focused on building something else. A company, art, you name it.

Like it or not, everyone’s a content creator now. That means who we are and what we make are often one and the same.

Among the countless creators and marketers out there, growth is daunting. Your audience only has so much attention to give.

With a compelling brand and consistent content, you give yourself a chance to shine. People don’t grow audiences or garner influence by accident. And both your personal brand and what you create sit within your control.

Relatability and authenticity matter to modern audiences

According to The 2025 Sprout Social Index™, consumers rank authenticity and relatability as two of the three most important brand content traits. Apply the same logic to individuals. This matters even more in an era where “influence” can feel manufactured.

That’s your edge as an individual. Nobody else has your experiences, your opinions or your sense of humor.

Making stronger connections with your community

Your voice and values shape your ability to grow your audience. Putting your personality front and center attracts like-minded followers.

That also means engaging with your audience to understand their needs and challenges. This goes hand in hand with establishing trust and building meaningful relationships.

When followers feel seen, they comment, share and come back for more. That’s how an audience becomes a community.

Opening doors to career and business opportunities

A strong personal brand puts your expertise on display before anyone asks for it. Recruiters, clients, collaborators and event organizers find you, instead of the other way around.

The 2025 Edelman-LinkedIn B2B Thought Leadership Impact Report found that thought leadership builds trust and opens doors where ads and traditional sales methods fall short. When you share your expertise in your own voice, you become the kind of thought leader buyers want to hear from.

What makes a strong personal brand?

A strong personal brand is specific, consistent and rooted in real value. Before you post anything, get well-defined answers to these questions.

  • Purpose: Why you’re building a brand at all (a new role, clients, a community or a product launch).

  • Niche: The narrow topic you want to be known for. Precision is memorable and breadth is forgettable.

  • Audience: The specific people you want to reach and the problems they need solved.

  • Value: What you give that audience that no one else does (expertise, perspective, entertainment or community).

  • Story: The experiences that explain why you care and why people should listen to you.
